content: Image resolution refers to the level of detail an image can convey. This concept applies to digital images, film images, and other types of visual media. Higher resolution indicates greater detail in the image. Resolution can be quantified in various ways, such as the number of lines per millimeter or inch, or the total number of lines in the height of an image (commonly referred to as TV lines). Additionally, line pairs are often used as a measurement, where a line pair consists of one dark line and one adjacent light line. For example, a resolution of 10 lines per millimeter corresponds to 5 dark lines alternating with 5 light lines, or 5 line pairs per millimeter. In photography, lens and film resolution are typically expressed in line pairs per millimeter. In digital imaging, resolution can be described in several ways. Pixel resolution is a common term, often used to refer to the pixel count of an image, although international standards discourage this usage in the context of digital cameras. An image with dimensions of N pixels in height and M pixels in width can have a resolution of up to N lines per picture height (or N TV lines). When pixel counts are referred to as resolution, they are typically expressed as two positive integers, such as 640 by 480, representing the number of pixel columns (width) and rows (height). Another convention is to describe resolution as the total number of pixels in the image, often given in megapixels, calculated by multiplying the pixel columns by the pixel rows and dividing by one million. Other methods include describing pixels per unit length (e.g., pixels per inch) or per unit area (e.g., pixels per square inch). For illustration purposes, images at different pixel resolutions may be displayed with sharp square pixels to emphasize the differences, although smooth image reconstruction is generally preferred. Spatial resolution measures how closely lines can be distinguished in an image. It depends on the properties of the imaging system, not just the pixel resolution (e.g., pixels per inch). The clarity of an image is determined by its spatial resolution rather than the total number of pixels. Spatial resolution refers to the number of independent pixel values per unit length. For example, computer monitors typically have spatial resolutions of 72 to 100 lines per inch, corresponding to pixel resolutions of 72 to 100 pixels per inch (ppi). In scanners, optical resolution is sometimes used to differentiate spatial resolution from pixel density. In geographic information systems (GIS), spatial resolution often refers to the ground sample distance (GSD), which indicates the area of Earth's surface covered by a single pixel. In astronomy, spatial resolution is measured in data points per arcsecond subtended at the observation point, as the physical distance between objects in the image depends on their distance from the observer. This measurement is crucial for detecting periodicity in specimens or visualizing interactions between individual atoms. Spectral resolution pertains to the ability of an image to distinguish light of different wavelengths or spectra. Multispectral images can resolve finer differences in wavelength than are necessary for reproducing color, offering higher spectral resolution. This capability is particularly useful in applications requiring detailed spectral analysis. Temporal resolution refers to the ability to resolve events occurring at different points in time. For example, movie cameras typically operate at 15 to 30 frames per second (fps), while high-speed cameras can achieve 100 to 1,000 fps or more. Some cameras and displays may offset color components relative to each other or mix temporal and spatial resolution, as seen in technologies like digital cameras, LCDs, and CRTs. Radiometric resolution determines how finely a system can represent or distinguish differences in intensity. It is usually expressed as the number of levels or bits, such as 8 bits or 256 levels, which is common in computer image files. Higher radiometric resolution allows for better representation of subtle differences in intensity or reflectivity, although in practice, the effective radiometric resolution is often limited by noise rather than the number of bits used for representation. Resolution varies across different media. For example, analog and digital formats have distinct resolution standards. In the NTSC system, Video CDs have a resolution of 350 × 240 (260 lines), while DVDs and digital formats like miniDV have resolutions of 720 × 480 (520 lines). High-definition formats such as Blu-ray and HDV offer resolutions of 1280 × 720 (720 lines) or 1920 × 1080 (1080 lines). IMAX and similar formats can achieve resolutions as high as 10,000 × 7,000 (7,000 lines). In film, 35mm motion picture film can resolve up to 6,000 lines in its original camera negative, while projection positives typically resolve around 2,000 lines due to the analog printing process. Modern film sequences are often scanned at resolutions of 2K, 4K, or even 8K for high-quality visual effects editing.
